basic_info.name: NAMASTE Portal (National Ayush Morbidity and Standardized Terminologies Electronic Portal)
basic_info.description: NAMASTE is the Ministry of Ayush's single-window, government-run web portal that publishes the standardized clinical terminologies and national morbidity codes for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani (ASU), together with WHO ICD-10 and ICD-11 reference tabs and a monthly aggregate-morbidity data-entry dashboard for Ayush hospitals. The single most load-bearing fact for MediKiosk is that it is the authoritative Indian source of AYUSH diagnosis vocabulary (2,895 National Ayurveda Morbidity Codes / NAMC, plus SAT-A through SAT-J terminology groups totalling 14,753 Ayurveda concepts, with separate Siddha and Unani sets), and that 1,941 of these ASU morbidity codes were formally mapped into WHO ICD-11 Chapter 26 Module 2 (Traditional Medicine Module 2, TM2), released on the WHO ICD-11 Browser in February 2025 under a WHO-Ministry of Ayush donor agreement spanning 2020-2025. The portal is a reporting and reference repository, not an interoperability service: it has no public API, no published FHIR CodeSystem/ValueSet and no downloadable official dataset, so the only standards-compatible way to put NAMASTE concepts into an ABDM/OPConsultRecord bundle is indirectly through the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension (NRCeS/CDAC) or via third-party/research FHIR wrappers. OPD records have no explicit Prakriti/Vikriti fields - NAMASTE carries morbidity diagnoses, not constitution (Prakriti) assessments, which live in the separate Ayusoft Prakriti Assessment Portal. As of the portal's 08-Sep-2026 update it reports 256 hospitals registered, 187 actually uploading, 12,119,333 OPD records since 2017 (~1.21 crore) and 160,502 IPD records.
basic_info.organization: Ministry of Ayush, Government of India owns and operates the portal and hosts it on the Ayush Grid (My Ayush Integrated Services Portal / MAISP). Terminology and morbidity-code content is developed by the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS), the Central Council for Research in Siddha (CCRS) and the Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine (CCRUM). The SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension is co-developed with and maintained by the National Resource Centre for EHR Standards (NRCeS), C-DAC Pune, under MoHFW; WHO is the partner on ICD-11 TM2. Site infrastructure is associated with BISAG-N.
basic_info.country: India (Government of India, Ministry of Ayush). Content and mandate are India-specific.
basic_info.status: Production / live government portal, actively maintained. The homepage shows a Last Update Version stamp of 08-Sep-2026 and a running OPD/IPD dashboard. It is in active programme expansion: the Ayush Grid case study and a July-2026 Lok Sabha answer report 6,245 Ayush health facilities onboarded onto the ABDM-compliant A-HMIS as of 31 July 2026, with NAMASTE codes and ICD-11 TM2 embedded as the diagnostic coding layer. The portal itself, however, remains a reference/statistics platform rather than a machine-consumable service.

technical_features.what_it_does: NAMASTE provides three functions. First, a browsable repository of standardized AYUSH terminologies and morbidity codes: Ayurveda is organised into SAT-A (basic/fundamental terms, 318), SAT-B (structure and function, 300), SAT-C (diagnosis and disorders, 175), SAT-D (signs and symptoms, 9,400), SAT-E (National Ayurveda Morbidity Codes, NAMC, 2,895), SAT-F (pharmacognosy, 565), SAT-G (medicine preparation, 197), SAT-H (food and beverages, 116), SAT-I (treatment, 663) and SAT-J (preventive/promotive health, 124), with parallel Siddha and Unani term sets (Unani ~4,028 terms; Siddha split across formulations, Noi Nadal pathology, Maruthuvam diseases, Gunapadam pharmacology and external therapies). Second, WHO reference tabs: embedded ICD-10 and ICD-11 browsers/coding tools so coders can assign both an ASU code and an ICD code (the 'double coding' scheme). Third, a data-entry and dashboard module where registered Ayush hospitals upload monthly aggregate OPD/IPD statistics disaggregated by ASU morbidity code and ICD-10, stratified by age and new-versus-repeat, with visualisation of trends and top-10 disorders. For Module C it matters as the vocabulary authority for AYUSH diagnoses and as the domestic/international harmonisation target (NAMC plus ICD-11 TM2 dual coding), not as a service the kiosk can call.
technical_features.architecture: Centralised government web application (accessible at namaste.ayush.gov.in; an older host namstp.ayush.gov.in also exists) with public browse pages, an authenticated sign-in/sign-up area for hospitals and practitioners, a 'NICE module', a 'Foundation Module' for double coding, a stats dashboard and sensitisation/training modules. It is hosted within the Ayush Grid / MAISP ecosystem and the site is associated with BISAG-N infrastructure. The morbidity-statistics workflow is deliberately low-tech: registered Healthcare Organisations fill Excel sheets of OPD/IPD data monthly and upload them. There is no documented public REST API, no FHIR terminology server endpoint, no published CodeSystem/ValueSet artifact and no official bulk dataset download; the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension is distributed separately through SNOMED International's MLDS under affiliate licensing. Third-party/research projects (AyushSyncAPI, CodexRaunak/NAMASTE-ICD-11-Integration) build FHIR R4 ConceptMap wrappers by scraping/ingesting NAMASTE CSVs and calling the WHO ICD-11 API.
technical_features.inputs: For the reference portal: human browsing/search of ASU terms and codes. For the statistics module: monthly aggregate OPD and IPD counts uploaded by registered Ayush hospitals as Excel sheets, coded to ASU morbidity codes and ICD-10 and stratified by age and new/repeat consultation. For downstream integration projects: NAMASTE code CSVs and the WHO ICD-11 API are the raw inputs used to construct mappings.
technical_features.outputs: Human-readable standardized terminologies and morbidity codes with Sanskrit/Tamil/Arabic-Persian-Urdu source terms, transliteration and English descriptions; dual-coded (ASU + ICD-10/11) guidance; aggregate statistical dashboards and top-disorder reports; and sensitisation/training material. It does not emit a clinical note, Composition, Bundle or FHIR CodeableConcept - FHIR representation only exists in external research microservices that wrap the vocabulary (e.g. ConceptMap 'namaste-icd11' with equivalent/relatedto equivalence flags) and in the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension used within EHR systems.
technical_features.standards_compliance: The portal's conformance is to classification and terminology standards, and is government-mandated rather than self-claimed, but it is not an HL7/FHIR artefact store. It aligns ASU morbidity codes (NAMC) with WHO ICD-10 and ICD-11, and 1,941 ASU codes were mapped into ICD-11 Chapter 26 Module 2 (TM2), released on the WHO ICD-11 Browser in February 2025, with the double-coding workflow designed to meet the WHO Minimum Data Set requirements. Its content feeds Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Ayush standards documents (at least five BIS documents are based on NAMASTE terminology) and is the source for the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension developed with NRCeS. There is NO published NAMASTE FHIR CodeSystem, ValueSet or ConceptMap from the Ministry, and NAMASTE codes are not directly referenced by the NRCeS FHIR IG for ABDM (v6.5.0), which binds AYUSH-relevant fields to SNOMED CT and other EHR-Standards-for-India terminologies. Any FHIR representation of NAMASTE today is third-party/research and not vendor-validated against the ABDM IG.
technical_features.offline_capability: None. NAMASTE is a network-dependent, centrally hosted web portal; both browsing and the monthly upload workflow require internet access and (for upload) authentication. No official offline bundle, downloadable dataset, local terminology package or store-and-forward mechanism is published. This is a material constraint for the offline-first kiosk: the AYUSH vocabulary must be obtained out-of-band (via the separately licensed SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension, BIS standards documents, or a scraped/derived code list) and embedded locally, because the portal itself will not be reachable at a disconnected kiosk.
technical_features.languages_supported: The portal interface is in English. Underlying term content carries original-language scripts and transliterations: Ayurveda terms in Sanskrit (Devanagari script plus IAST diacritics), Siddha terms in Tamil script with roman diacritics, and Unani terms in Arabic, Persian and Urdu scripts ('Alawi Nasta'liq), each with transliteration and (often) an English description or equivalent. The SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension translates terms into Sanskrit, Tamil and Urdu respectively. There is no evidence of a Hindi-specific or Hinglish UI, and no patient-facing bilingual rendering is offered by NAMASTE itself.
technical_features.deployment_model: Government cloud / central web portal hosted under the Ayush Grid (MAISP), reached over the internet through a standard browser; data entry by hospitals via Excel upload. There is no on-device, kiosk, LAN or room-server deployment model, and no published hardware requirements because it is not software that an implementer installs. For MediKiosk the only viable integration is to embed a local copy of the codes/terminology (obtained under the applicable SNOMED CT or BIS terms) rather than to deploy NAMASTE.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: No accuracy, F1 or concordance metrics are applicable or published, because NAMASTE is a controlled vocabulary/classification rather than a model. The only quality-relevant published evidence is coverage/utilisation: an initial evaluation (J Res Ayurvedic Sci, 2024) reported that of 2,888 National Ayurveda Morbidity Codes then listed, 2,470 were actually used by reporting HCOs, based on 61,92,458 (6.19 million) Ayurvedic treatment records from 133 registered Ayurvedic HCOs as of August 2023 - i.e. real-world code usage covers a majority but not all of the code set. The 2026 NAMASTE-ICD-11 mapping work reports 1,941 ASU morbidity codes mapped to ICD-11 TM2.
performance_metrics.latency: Not applicable / not published. NAMASTE exposes no programmatic service with benchmarked latency. Third-party FHIR wrappers report 'low latency translation performance' only for synthetic datasets in research settings, which is not a production figure and not attributable to the portal.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Not applicable to the portal (central government hosting). The practical resource implication for Module C is indirect: any local NAMASTE/SAT/NAMC subset or SNOMED CT AYUSH Extension package embedded on the kiosk should be small enough for the ~4GB CPU/iGPU budget - the Ayurveda NAMC set is only 2,895 codes and the full Ayurveda terminology is 14,753 concepts, so a local lookup table or lightweight terminology index is trivial relative to LLM/model footprints. The constraint is licensing and data acquisition, not compute.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Portal-reported as of the 08-Sep-2026 update: 256 hospitals registered, 187 uploading data, 12,119,333 OPD records since 2017 (~1.21 crore), 2,321,705 additional OPD/outreach records, and 160,502 IPD records since 2017. Historical baseline (2023) was 133 Ayurvedic HCOs and 6.19 million Ayurvedic treatment records. The wider delivery platform A-HMIS had 6,245 Ayush health facilities onboarded as of 31 July 2026. These are modest relative to the OPD volumes of mainstream Indian hospitals and indicate that NAMASTE-native digital capture is still early-stage.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Not a model benchmark. Evaluation evidence consists of peer-reviewed descriptive/statistical assessments of portal data (e.g. the 2024 NAMASTE data-analysis paper on code usage across states) and government programme reporting; terminology mapping to ICD-11 TM2 was a formal WHO-partnered process (donor agreement, WHO ICD-11 Browser release, Feb 2025) rather than an ML evaluation. There is no accuracy, safety or concordance benchmark and no independent audit of the portal's data quality published.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: NAMASTE is the vocabulary supply for the AYUSH half of Module C's summary. The NRCeS OPConsultRecord profile has no dedicated AYUSH sections - there is no standard 'Prakriti' or 'Vikriti' slot - so any Ayurveda/Siddha/Unani diagnosis the kiosk records must be carried inside existing OPConsultRecord sections (most plausibly a Condition/diagnosis entry or an investigation/other section), and it must be coded with something the ABDM FHIR IG accepts. NAMASTE supplies the domestic code set (NAMC, SAT groups) and the harmonisation target (ICD-11 TM2, mapped for 1,941 ASU codes since Feb 2025), giving MediKiosk a dual-coding story that is both nationally standard and internationally comparable. It also clarifies the Prakriti/Vikriti gap: NAMASTE is a morbidity/diagnosis classification, not a constitution (Prakriti) assessment terminology - Prakriti profiles come from the separate Ayusoft Prakriti Assessment Portal integrated with A-HMIS - so Module C must treat constitutional assessment and disease coding as two different data elements with two different sources.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) dual coding as the AYUSH strategy - record the ASU diagnosis code (NAMC/SAT) alongside ICD-11 TM2 and any biomedical ICD/SNOMED mapping, because that is the Ministry's own national model and it future-proofs the summary for A-HMIS/ABDM reporting; (2) the local embedding of the NAMC 2,895-code set plus relevant SAT groups as a lightweight offline lookup table, since it is tiny relative to the 4GB budget and eliminates portal dependency; (3) ICD-11 TM2 codes as the internationally recognised representation for mapped ASU conditions, since TM2 is now live on the WHO browser. Adopt with caution / adapt: use the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension as the FHIR-facing coding vehicle where the ABDM IG demands SNOMED CT, since NAMASTE codes are not themselves IG-bound. Reject: (1) any design that assumes NAMASTE can be queried at runtime from the kiosk (no API, no offline bundle); (2) relying on the portal's aggregate statistics module as a data source - it is monthly, aggregate and reporting-oriented, not patient-level; (3) presenting Prakriti/Vikriti as NAMASTE-coded fields, because they are not in the morbidity code sets.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Key risks for Module C: NAMASTE has no public API, no published FHIR artifacts and no official downloadable dataset - a 2026 research paper explicitly states the official NAMASTE dataset 'was not readily available' and had to be replaced with a synthetic CodeSystem - so integrating it is a scrape/extract-and-license exercise, not a service integration. Licensing is not clearly stated on the portal: the page content is 'owned by Ministry of Ayush', with no explicit open-data licence, and the standards-compatible route (SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension) carries SNOMED affiliate-sublicensing obligations via MLDS, which is a real compliance item for a commercial/competition kiosk. Coverage is incomplete: only 187 of 256 registered hospitals actually upload, the code set is geared to morbidity/reason-for-encounter rather than constitutional assessment, and the portal's statistics are aggregate and lag patient-level EHR needs. There is a real risk that ASU diagnoses entered on the kiosk are unmappable to any ABDM-acceptable code if they are not in the 1,941-code TM2 mapping or the SNOMED AYUSH Extension, forcing a free-text or unmapped fallback that weakens the 'structured' claim of the summary.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: NAMASTE is a standards body/vocabulary authority, not a competitor, and it strengthens MediKiosk's differentiation on the NRCeS-conformant emission and India-residency axes by supplying an accredited, government-owned AYUSH coding layer that a generic international intake/summarisation tool would not use. It does not erode any MediKiosk differentiator: it does no elicitation, no summarisation, no document digitisation, no physician attestation and no FHIR emission. The gap it exposes is one MediKiosk can own: because the OPConsultRecord has no native AYUSH/Prakriti sections and NAMASTE is not IG-bound, a kiosk that can reliably capture, dual-code and provenance-tag AYUSH diagnoses into an ABDM-acceptable bundle solves a problem neither the portals nor the mainstream scribes address.

business_info.license: NAMASTE is a Government of India public portal; its website states content is 'owned by Ministry of Ayush, Government of India' with no separate open-source or open-data licence file published, so reuse terms are not explicitly granted. The standards-compatible derivative used by EHRs - the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension - is distributed under SNOMED International affiliate licensing through the Member Licensing and Distribution Service (MLDS), which governs sublicensing for products built on it. BIS Ayush standards documents based on NAMASTE are separately published standards. [uncertain] A specific, machine-readable reuse licence for the NAMASTE code lists could not be confirmed from the portal itself.
business_info.pricing: Free to use / view as a public government service; there is no subscription or paid tier for portal access. Costs arise indirectly through SNOMED CT affiliate licensing/sublicensing for the AYUSH Extension and through procurement of BIS standards documents.
business_info.funding: Publicly funded by the Government of India through the Ministry of Ayush, with the ICD-11 TM2 work formalised under a WHO-Ministry of Ayush donor agreement (2020-2025). No commercial funding or private backing.
business_info.commercial_status: Government programme / public good, not a commercial product. It is an official Ministry of Ayush digital asset within the Ayush Grid.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Not a competitor but adjacent vocabulary/classification options: WHO ICD-11 Traditional Medicine Module 2 (TM2), which is the international classification NAMASTE maps into; the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension (NRCeS/C-DAC), which is the SNOMED-facing representation of the same ASU concepts and the more directly usable option for FHIR-coded EHRs; the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Traditional Medicine; and China's TCM classifications (ICD-11 TM1), which are the parallel international analogue. Third-party integration tools (AyushSyncAPI, CodexRaunak/NAMASTE-ICD-11-Integration) compete to be the practical API/FHIR layer that NAMASTE itself does not provide.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: NAMASTE codes and ICD-11 TM2 are embedded in the ABDM-compliant Ayush Hospital Management Information System (A-HMIS) as the dual-coding diagnostic layer, which also integrates ABHA IDs and HPR IDs, the Ayusoft Prakriti Assessment Portal, the e-Samhita classical-reference portal and the Ayush Research Portal. It links to the Central Bureau of Health Intelligence, National Health Mission and National Ayush Health Mission for reporting, and the portal sits inside the My Ayush Integrated Services Portal (MAISP) / Ayush Grid. It connects to NRCeS for the SNOMED CT AYUSH Extension and to WHO for ICD-11 TM2. There is no direct NAMASTE-to-NRCeS-FHIR-IG integration.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: The Ayush Grid is explicitly aligning with ABDM and building FHIR-based APIs, with NAMASTE morbidity codes and ICD-11 TM2 as the semantic layer, which is a tailwind for any AYUSH-conformant kiosk: the Ministry is actively pushing dual coding, ABHA/HPR identity and A-HMIS expansion (6,245 facilities as of July 2026). A-HMIS being an ABDM-compliant EHR means an emitted AYUSH summary has a plausible downstream home. The gaps to design around are the absence of an official NAMASTE FHIR terminology service and the licensing path via SNOMED CT - both of which point to using the SNOMED CT India AYUSH Extension (via MLDS) plus locally embedded NAMASTE/ICD-11 TM2 code lists rather than depending on the portal at runtime. Government emphasis on multilingual support via BHASHINI also aligns with MediKiosk's bilingual requirement.

history.release_date: 2017-10-17. The NAMASTE Portal was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the 2nd Ayurveda Day at the All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi.
history.key_milestones: 2016-2017: terminology harmonisation accelerated under the CCRAS 'Harmonization of Ayurveda Terminologies' working group, culminating in the NAMASTE portal launch (17 Oct 2017). Nov 2018: real-time double coding introduced in A-HMIS across 100 hospitals. 2020-2025: WHO-funded/partnered programme to standardise and map ASU morbidity codes. Jan 2024: Ministry of Ayush and WHO event in New Delhi (10 Jan 2024) announcing the ASU morbidity codes as ICD-11 TM Chapter Module 2, under a signed donor agreement. Feb 2025: ICD-11 TM2 officially released on the WHO ICD-11 Browser, with 1,941 ASU national morbidity codes mapped. 2025-2026: Ayush Grid/A-HMIS expansion and academic work (2026) proposing FHIR-compliant API frameworks and dual-coding EMR integrations for NAMASTE + ICD-11 TM2.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: The six-month window (Mar-Sep 2026) shows continued but incremental activity rather than a major portal relaunch. The homepage now carries a Last Update Version stamp of 08-Sep-2026. Two 2026 papers advanced the interoperability conversation: an IJACTE article (20 May 2026) analysing NAMASTE-ICD-11 integration and proposing API-based, FHIR-compliant exchange and AI-assisted terminology alignment, and an RRJoMST article (published 27 Aug 2026) building a FHIR-enabled NAMASTE + ICD-11 TM2 terminology service on a synthetic CodeSystem because the official dataset was not available. A June 2026 Zenodo paper framed the same dual-coding/FHIR microservice approach. Government reporting (Lok Sabha answer, late 2026) stated 6,245 Ayush facilities onboarded on AHMIS as of 31 July 2026, with continued ABDM alignment, multilingual support via BHASHINI, and AI/ML adoption planned. No new public NAMASTE API or FHIR artifact release was identified; the FHIR representation remains research/third-party.

market_positioning.target_users: Ayush students, practitioners, medical record and coding personnel, hospital administrators, public health experts and policy makers; registered Ayush Healthcare Organisations that upload monthly morbidity statistics; and the wider Ayush Grid / ABDM digital-health ecosystem (A-HMIS vendors, EHR implementers). Patients are not direct users.
market_positioning.market_segment: AYUSH clinical terminology, disease classification and morbidity reporting (health informatics standards). It is not intake, ambient scribing, PHR or a diagnostics kiosk product - it is the vocabulary/classification layer beneath those.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: The portal presents itself as the 'National Ayush Morbidity and Standardized Terminologies Electronic Portal', a 'comprehensive web-portal for Standardized Terminologies and National Morbidity Codes of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Systems of Medicine and WHO-ICD-10 and ICD-11'. Its stated mission is pan-India implementation of ASU National Morbidity Codes with dual coding alongside ICD-10/11, ICD coding for Yoga/Naturopathy/Homoeopathy, and serving as the reference repository for developing A-S-U international terminologies and ICD-11 morbidity codes. The Ministry frames it as a landmark event bringing AYUSH 'equity with mainstream health care system'.
